cards.back: **Modelling** = creation, manipulation and storage of **geometric objects** — shape, structure, properties. **Rendering** = generating their **images** via lighting, shading, texturing and rasterization. Modelling lives in object coordinates; rendering is the journey through world/eye/clip/NDC/window.

cards.front: The seven applications of computer graphics
cards.back: **Data visualization** (graphs, charts) · **CAD** · **VR environments** · **Education & training** · **Entertainment** (animation, games) · **Image processing** · **GUIs**.

cards.front: What does an API do in a graphics system?
cards.back: It **connects an application program to the graphics system**. **Software drivers then convert API output to hardware-specific instructions** — so your program never needs to know which GPU it is talking to.

**`moveto(x,y)`** — move without drawing. **`lineto(x,y)`** — draw from the current position. Precise vector output (drafting, CNC). **Limits:** doesn't extend to 3D, no real-time rendering, slower than raster displays. Note it is **stateful** — the ancestor of OpenGL's state machine.

**`write_pixel(x, y, color)`** — directly manipulates the **framebuffer**. **Pros:** fine control, shading/anti-aliasing/texturing, blending and filtering. **Cons:** pixelates on resize, no structural information about objects, memory-intensive.

cards.front: The four components a 3D API must specify
cards.back: **Objects** (sets of vertices) · **Viewer** (camera position & orientation) · **Light sources** (directional, spot, point) · **Material properties** (absorption, scattering, diffuse/specular). Exactly what's needed to answer *'what colour is this pixel?'* Examples: OpenGL, Direct3D, Open Scene Graph.

cards.front: What is a display list, and what is its modern equivalent?
cards.back: **Image instructions stored in memory and executed repeatedly** to maintain the display without flicker — freeing the CPU from re-describing the picture each refresh. Modern equivalent: the **vertex buffer object (VBO)** — upload once, one draw call per frame.

cards.front: The four major steps of the imaging process
cards.back: **① Vertex processing** — transform each vertex, compute lighting. **② Clipping & primitive assembly** — discard what's outside the view volume, at the primitive level. **③ Rasterization** — primitives become **fragments**. **④ Fragment processing** — texture, bump map, hidden-surface removal, final colour.

A **fragment is a candidate** pixel carrying colour, depth and texture data. It may be **discarded** by the depth or alpha test, or **blended** with others — several fragments can compete for one pixel. They are not the same thing.

cards.front: Why is a pipeline the right architecture for graphics?
cards.back: Every vertex undergoes the **same sequence of independent operations**. A deep pipeline produces one finished vertex per clock once full; independence also allows **thousands in parallel**. Deep pipelining + massive parallelism = why a GPU beats a CPU here.

**Fixed-function**: a predefined path; you set *parameters* (`glEnable`, `glLight*`); one built-in lighting model. **Programmable**: you supply **the code that runs** at the vertex and fragment stages. Clipping and rasterization stay fixed — pure geometry, no artistic decisions.

cards.front: What do vertex and fragment shaders each do?
cards.back: **Vertex shader** (per vertex): modify positions for **morphing/deformation/animation**, compute vertex colours from lighting, perform **custom transformations**. **Fragment shader** (per fragment): **textures, transparency, bump mapping, shading**, advanced lighting, reflections and refractions.

cards.front: Why prefer per-vertex work over per-fragment work?
cards.back: A full-screen triangle at 1080p has **3 vertices and ~2 million fragments**. Work done per-vertex and **interpolated** by the rasterizer is thousands of times cheaper. This single fact drives most real-time graphics optimisation.

**The entire Unit 1 coordinate pipeline in one line** — object coordinates in, clip coordinates out. The hardware then does the perspective divide and viewport transform. Everything about frames, homogeneous coordinates and concatenation compresses into that one matrix.

cards.front: How does a 2D point map into 3D?
cards.back: $p = (x,y)$ becomes $(x, y, 0)$ — which is why there is **no separate 2D graphics system**. In homogeneous form: $(x,y,0,1)$, with $w=1$ because it's a **point**.

**World** — global, fixed origin $(0,0,0)$. **Object** — local to one model, defines its shape. **Physical-device (NDC)** — normalized, **$[-1,1]$ in OpenGL**, device-independent. **Window/screen** — final pixel coordinates. ⚠ The **full** OpenGL pipeline has **six** (adds eye and clip).

$x_{\text{screen}} = \frac{(x_{\text{ndc}}+1)}{2}W$ and $y_{\text{screen}} = \frac{(y_{\text{ndc}}+1)}{2}H$ — maps the canonical $[-1,1]$ cube onto actual pixels. It is why the same scene fills the screen at any resolution.

1. Start with a triangle; pick a point $p$ **inside** it. 2. Select one of the three vertices **at random**; find $q$ = **midpoint** of $p$ and that vertex. 3. Plot $q$; set $p = q$. 4. Repeat. Despite the randomness the result is **highly ordered and self-similar**.

cards.front: Why does the random gasket algorithm work?
cards.back: The midpoint step is the **affine sum** $q = \frac12 p + \frac12 V$ — a convex combination, so $q$ stays inside the triangle. The map halves every distance, pulling points onto the fractal **attractor**. This is the **Chaos Game**, the simplest iterated function system.

**① Immediate** — draw each point as generated: one call per point. **② Store then display** — accumulate, then one bulk draw. **③ GPU** — upload once to GPU memory, then a **single draw call** replays it. ③ eliminates per-frame CPU→GPU traffic — the display-list idea as a VBO.

Subdivide a triangle at its edge midpoints into 4 sub-triangles, **discard the middle one**, recurse on the other 3 → $3^n$ triangles at depth $n$. The **3D version** uses a **tetrahedron**, discarding the centre → $4^n$ tetrahedra.

cards.front: The six categories of API functions
cards.back: **① Primitive** (lines, polygons, triangles, quads) · **② Attribute** (colours, fills) · **③ Viewing** (camera, ortho/perspective) · **④ Transformation** (rotate, translate, scale, shear) · **⑤ Input** (keyboard, mouse, tablets) · **⑥ Control** (multiprocessing, multi-window, error handling).

**GL** — the core Graphics Library: 2D/3D rendering functions. **GLEW** — OpenGL **Extension Wrangler**: manages extensions, removes platform-specific dependencies. **GLUT** — OpenGL **Utility Toolkit**: **window management, input handling, event-driven main loop**. OpenGL itself handles no OS-specific tasks.

cards.front: How to read an OpenGL function name
cards.back: `glVertex3fv` → `gl` (library) + `Vertex` (operation) + **`3`** (component count) + **`f`** (type: f float, d double, i int, s short) + **`v`** (arguments passed as a **vector/array**). Prefixes: `gl` core · `glu` utility · `glut` toolkit.

cards.front: Why is OpenGL called a state machine?
cards.back: Current colour, current matrix, bound buffer and dozens of other settings are **global state that persists until changed** — so the same drawing code produces different output depending on what ran before. The discipline is to **push/pop state** around anything you change.

**Points** (single location) · **Line segments** (two endpoints) · **Polygons** (closed, triangles/quads most common) · **Curves** (Bézier, splines) · **Surfaces** (patches, meshes). They pass through the **geometric pipeline**: transform, clip, light, shade.

**Geometric**: vertices + topology, transformable, resolution-independent, go through the **geometric pipeline**. **Raster**: arrays of pixels in the framebuffer, **no** definable points/edges/transforms in 3D, follow a separate **rasterization pipeline** (blending, filtering, anti-aliasing).

**`GL_LINES`** — independent segments, vertices consumed **in pairs**. **`GL_LINE_STRIP`** — connected open path $(v_0v_1),(v_1v_2),\dots$ **`GL_LINE_LOOP`** — the strip **plus a closing segment** back to $v_0$.

$n$ vertices give $n-2$ triangles. Drawing 100 connected triangles needs **300 vertices with `GL_TRIANGLES` but only 102 with `GL_TRIANGLE_STRIP`** — roughly 3× less per-vertex work. The same 'stop re-sending data' instinct as display lists and VBOs.

cards.front: The performance metric for polygon rendering
cards.back: **Polygons rendered per second.** Higher throughput = more detail; lower = lag and dropped frames. In VR it matters ~3× more: **two eyes at 90 fps** instead of one at 60.

**① Render edges only** — wireframe; cheap; for debugging and modelling. **② Render the interior** with solid colour/gradient/pattern — flat shading or texturing; **most common in real-time and games**. **③ Selectively render edges** — cel-shading outlines for stylisation; removing edges for photo-realism.

**Simple** — no two non-adjacent edges intersect; unambiguous interior. **Complex** — self-intersecting or holed; interior needs a fill rule. **OpenGL assumes simple, convex, planar polygons and does not check** — feed it otherwise and behaviour is undefined.

**① Always planar** (3 points define a plane). **② Always convex** — never self-intersecting. **③ Trivial to rasterize** — three edge functions. **④ Barycentric interpolation is natural** — the affine-sum weights from Unit 1. Everything else is tessellated into triangles anyway.

`glutInit` → `glutInitWindowSize`/`Position`/`DisplayMode` → `glutCreateWindow` → **register callbacks** (`glutDisplayFunc`…) → **`glutMainLoop()`**. ⚠ `glutMainLoop()` **never returns** — code after it never runs. Default window size if unset: **300 × 300**.

`glutDisplayFunc` (redraw) · `glutKeyboardFunc` (key) · `glutMouseFunc` (button) · `glutMotionFunc` (drag) · `glutReshapeFunc` (resize) · `glutIdleFunc` (animation). `glutPostRedisplay()` schedules a redraw. These are API categories **⑤ input** and **⑥ control**.

`glPushMatrix()` saves a **copy of the current matrix** on a stack; `glPopMatrix()` restores it. Gives **scoped transformations** so a transform doesn't leak into subsequent objects — or into the next frame, since `display` runs repeatedly.

cards.front: Two bugs in the course's coloured-cube listing
cards.back: **① `glOrtho` then `gluPerspective`** without `glLoadIdentity()` between — both multiply into the same matrix, so the projection is neither. **② No push/pop around `glTranslatef`** — the translation accumulates into the model-view matrix and the second cube drifts each frame.

**Eye** (where the camera is) · **Centre** (what it looks at) · **Up** (which way is up). Eye fixes position, centre fixes direction, **up pins the remaining roll freedom** — six DOF total. ⚠ Up must **not** be parallel to the view direction, or the view matrix degenerates.

**Point source** — radiates equally in all directions. **Distributed (area)** — emits from a surface; soft shadows. **Spotlight** — a point source restricted to a cone. **Near vs far** — for a **far/directional** source all rays are parallel and the direction is computed **once**; a near source needs it per vertex plus attenuation.

**Diffuse** — scattered equally in all directions; depends on $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf l$; **view-independent**; gives matte. **Specular** — mirror-like reflection toward the viewer; **depends on viewing direction**, so the highlight **slides as you move** — which is what reads as *shiny*.

**Modeler** (defines objects) → **Interface file** (object descriptions, light sources, viewer location) → **Renderer** (generates the image). Modern form: **Blender → glTF → Three.js**. The file is the seam, which is why the halves can be different programs.

Both are **parallel** (projectors stay parallel). **Orthographic** — projectors **perpendicular** to the view plane; no distortion; front/top/side views (elevation/plan/profile). **Oblique** — projectors at **another angle**; distorted but measurable; shows multiple faces at once.

**Cavalier** — **full depth preserved** (scale 1.0), looks stretched. **Cabinet** — **depth scaled down** (0.5), looks natural. Cabinet fakes just enough foreshortening to satisfy the eye without giving up measurability.

cards.front: Where is parallel projection still used in AR/VR?
cards.back: **UI overlays, HUDs and magic-lens annotations** are drawn with an **orthographic** projection so they keep constant on-screen size regardless of distance. A headset renders the world in perspective and the interface in ortho, in the same frame.

cards.front: Where does perspective shrinking come from?
cards.back: Similar triangles give $x_p = -d\,x/z$ — the **division by $z$**. Double the depth and the projected size halves. Homogeneous coordinates arrange for $w$ to carry $z$, and the **perspective divide** at clip → NDC performs it.

**One point** — a single vanishing point; hallways, roads, railway tracks. **Two point** — two points on the horizon; buildings, furniture. **Three point** — a third above/below the horizon; skyscrapers, aerial views. **One vanishing point per receding axis.**

cards.front: Parallel vs perspective — the row that explains all the others
cards.back: **Distance from the centre of projection is INFINITE for parallel, FINITE for perspective.** Parallel projection *is* perspective with the eye moved infinitely far away — at which point projectors become parallel and foreshortening vanishes. Everything else in the table follows.

`glOrtho(l,r,b,t,n,f)` — a **rectangular box** view volume, parallel projectors, no depth effect; for CAD and UI. `gluPerspective(fovy, aspect, near, far)` — a **frustum**, converging projectors, distant objects shrink; for realistic 3D and VR. ⚠ Never call both without `glLoadIdentity()` between.

Depth-buffer precision is distributed **non-linearly** — most of it near the camera. A tiny `near` value starves distant geometry of precision, producing **z-fighting** (surfaces flickering as the depth test flips). Especially visible and unpleasant in VR.

**Scene** (scene-graph root) · **Camera** (viewer) · **Renderer** (draws scene from camera into a canvas). A visible object is a **Mesh = Geometry + Material**. `PerspectiveCamera(fov, aspect, near, far)` takes exactly `gluPerspective`'s arguments.
**① No light** while using a lit material (Standard/Phong/Lambert) — `MeshBasicMaterial` always shows. **② Camera inside the object** — both default to the origin. **③ Render loop never started.**

**The scene graph itself.** A child's transform is automatically relative to its parent, and the world matrix of any node is the product of every matrix up the chain to the root — Unit 1's frame composition, made structural rather than manual.

Set `camera.aspect`, call **`camera.updateProjectionMatrix()`** (the matrix is cached — changing `aspect` alone does nothing), then `renderer.setSize(...)`. The equivalent of forgetting `glutReshapeFunc`.

**Basic** — unlit, cheapest, for UI/debug. **Lambert** — diffuse only, per-vertex. **Phong** — diffuse + specular, per-fragment. **Standard** — PBR (roughness/metalness), the sensible default. **Physical** — PBR + clearcoat/transmission/sheen, most expensive.

Typed arrays of vertex attributes uploaded to the GPU — **this is the vertex buffer object**. `setAttribute('position', new BufferAttribute(arr, 3))`, where `3` is components per vertex — the same idea as the `3` in `glVertex3f`. **Indexed geometry** reuses vertices via an index buffer.

cards.front: Which texture maps are sRGB and which are linear?
cards.back: **sRGB: colour maps only** — `map`, `emissiveMap`. **Linear: data maps** — `normalMap`, `roughnessMap`, `metalnessMap`, `aoMap`, `displacementMap`. Data maps store **numbers, not colours**; tagging them sRGB silently corrupts the lighting.

**normalMap** fakes detail by **perturbing normals** — costs nothing geometrically but the **silhouette stays flat**. **displacementMap** genuinely **moves vertices**, changing the silhouette, but needs a **densely segmented geometry** to have anything to move. normalMap is the descendant of **bump mapping**.

**JavaScript's garbage collector cannot free GPU memory.** Removing a mesh releases the JS object but leaves buffers and textures resident on the GPU — a genuine leak in a long AR/VR session. `geometry.dispose()`, `material.dispose()`, `texture.dispose()`.

`rotation.y += 0.01` gives 0.6 rad/s at 60 fps but **1.44 rad/s at 144 fps** — different speeds on different machines. Use `+= 1.0 * delta` for one radian per **second**. Critical in VR, where headsets run at 72/90/120 Hz. ⚠ `clock.getDelta()` **resets the timer** — call it once per frame.

**Clip** — the authored keyframe data ('Walk', 'Idle'), arriving from glTF. **Mixer** — the per-model player, advanced by `mixer.update(delta)`. **Action** — one clip on one mixer; has `play()`, `fadeIn()`, weight, loop mode. `crossFadeTo` blends between clips.

**Step → copy → render.** `world.step()` advances the simulation; copy `body.translation()` and `body.rotation()` onto the mesh's `position` and **`quaternion`**; then render. The physics world owns position/orientation truth; Three.js owns appearance.

**Dynamic** — moves, affected by forces (falling objects). **Fixed/static** — never moves (floors, walls). **Kinematic** — you set its position; unaffected by forces (moving platforms, **the VR controller**). Colliders are **simplified convex shapes**, not the render mesh — the Unit 1 convex-hull argument.

Integrators are stable only at a constant step (~1/60 s). A variable delta makes behaviour hardware-dependent and can explode at low frame rates. Use an **accumulator**: `while (acc >= 1/60) { world.step(); acc -= 1/60; }` — decoupling physics rate from render rate.

cards.front: Where does Blender sit in the pipeline?
cards.back: It is **the modeller** in the modelling–rendering paradigm: **Blender → glTF/.glb (interface file) → Three.js (renderer)**. The 1990s architecture, unchanged, is the modern web-AR workflow.

**Block out** → **box modelling** (extrude, loop cut, bevel, inset) → **modifiers** (subdivision, mirror, array — non-destructive) → **UV unwrap** → **texture/shade** (Principled BSDF) → **rig** (armature + weights) → **animate** → **export .glb**.

cards.front: What is UV unwrapping and why does it matter?
cards.back: **Flattening the 3D surface into a 2D layout** so textures can be mapped onto it — mark **seams**, unwrap, arrange the **UV islands**. Distortion in the layout shows as stretched texture. ⚠ **A model with no UVs cannot be textured** — it renders flat-coloured whatever maps you assign.

**Armature** — a bone hierarchy (a scene graph; each bone's transform relative to its parent). **Skinning/weight painting** — each vertex gets **weights** saying how much each bone influences it, so the mesh deforms smoothly. **IK** — pose a chain by moving its end; **FK** — rotate each joint in turn.

**Apply transforms** · **triangulate** · **use Principled BSDF** (arbitrary node graphs don't export) · **bake procedural materials to textures** · **check polycount** · **pack textures into .glb** · **name animations** · **set the origin** where the pivot should be. ⚠ Blender is **Z-up**, glTF/Three.js are **Y-up**.

A **React renderer for Three.js** that builds **real Three.js objects** from a declarative component tree — not a wrapper or rewrite. Every Three.js class becomes a lower-case JSX element (`THREE.Mesh` → `<mesh>`), and the whole namespace is available automatically.

**`args={[...]}`** → arguments to the **constructor**: `args={[1,1,1]}` is `new BoxGeometry(1,1,1)`. **Ordinary props** → values **set on the instance**: `position`, `rotation`, `color`, `roughness`. Nesting expresses both the scene graph and attachment.

cards.front: What does <Canvas> provide, and what does R3F give free?
cards.back: `<Canvas>` creates **scene, camera, renderer and render loop** in one element. Free: **`useFrame`** (with delta), **pointer events** with no manual Raycaster, **automatic resize**, **automatic disposal on unmount**, and React-state-driven scene contents.

It triggers a React re-render **up to 120 times a second**. Mutate through a **ref** instead (`ref.current.rotation.y += delta`). **State = things that change occasionally** (hovered, selected); **refs = things that change every frame**.

cards.front: What is WebXR and what does it give you?
cards.back: The browser standard for **headsets, AR phones and controllers** (replacing WebVR). It provides the **headset pose each frame**, **one viewport + projection matrix per eye**, **controller/hand poses**, a **reference space**, and **hit testing**. You still provide the scene and the rendering.

cards.front: The one-line change that breaks WebXR ports
cards.back: **`requestAnimationFrame` must become `renderer.setAnimationLoop`.** In an immersive session the **headset drives frame timing** (72/90/120 Hz), independent of the browser's refresh. Keeping rAF means the loop stops or runs at the wrong rate.

**`inline`** — in-page, non-immersive. **`immersive-vr`** — the real world is replaced. **`immersive-ar`** — the real world is **visible behind** the content, so the clear colour must be **transparent** (no skybox). This is Unit 3's AR-vs-VR distinction as an API flag.

**`viewer`** — origin at the headset. **`local`** — roughly where the user started; seated. **`local-floor`** — $y=0$ is the **real floor**; standing. **`bounded-floor`** — floor plus a safe polygon. **`unbounded`** — world-scale, may drift. Wrong choice ⇒ 'everything is the wrong height'.

The browser casts a ray from the device **into its model of the real world** and reports where it lands — floor, table, wall. It powers every 'tap to place' AR app, and depends on the device's **SLAM-based world model**, which Unit 4 explains. Requires `requiredFeatures: ['hit-test']`.

**① `pose` can be null** — tracking is lost when the headset is covered or the user leaves the tracked area; hold the last pose rather than snapping to the origin. **② WebXR requires a secure context** — HTTPS or `localhost`; over plain HTTP it silently reports no XR support.
